On ordering structure: bundled plate packs suit most new fit-outs, delivering a defined weight range across every platform at a predictable budget. Custom weight-range ordering makes more sense where platforms serve distinct programming streams and a standard bundle would leave certain denominations unused. Browse MasterKraft's commercial weightlifting equipment for available plate configurations before finalising your order structure.

![Commercial vs. Home Gym Spec: Why the Difference Matters More Than the Price Tag](/blog-images/xBAfer3OTW2CZE7t4i7lP.webp "Commercial vs. Home Gym Spec: Why the Difference Matters More Than the Price Tag")

## Commercial vs. Home Gym Spec: Why the Difference Matters More Than the Price Tag

Plate type tells you what you're buying. Spec grade tells you whether it survives your facility.

Plates priced well below commercial grade may look attractive until they fail under daily commercial load long before a commercial-grade equivalent would. The price tag is the wrong comparison point; total cost of ownership is the right one.

The failure modes that accelerate under commercial use are specific. Hub separation occurs when high-frequency drops fatigue the bond between the steel insert and rubber body, a process that plays out far faster on a busy strength floor than in a home gym. Rubber delamination follows a similar pattern, driven by cumulative impact cycles rather than any single event. Dimensional drift is less visible but operationally damaging: plates that creep outside their original tolerances create inconsistent bar loading across your platforms over time.

Member volume is the variable most operators underestimate. A plate rated for home gym use is not engineered for the session frequency of a busy commercial floor across multiple platforms. That is not a marginal difference in wear; it is a structural mismatch. For more on matching equipment grade to actual usage load, this guide to specifying commercial gym equipment in Australia works through the framework in full.

There is also a liability dimension that sits outside the equipment budget entirely. Specifying sub-commercial equipment in a commercial facility can create exposure with your insurer and complicate your obligations under Australian workplace health and safety requirements if equipment fails during member use.

**To calculate a cost-per-drop benchmark:** estimate your daily class or open-floor sessions, multiply by average drops per session, then divide your plate purchase cost by projected total drops over a three-year period. Compare that figure across product tiers rather than comparing sticker prices.

## What to Ask Any Supplier Before You Place an Order

Once you've assessed the spec, the next question is whether the supplier can actually deliver, literally and operationally.

**Get service commitments in writing.** A verbal assurance is worthless when a delivery is short 200 kg of plates two days before a facility opens. Ask specifically: what is the documented response time if a product fails or an order arrives incomplete? A measurable SLA, such as a 72-hour resolution commitment, is different from goodwill. If a supplier cannot produce it in writing, treat that as a data point.

**Confirm actual stock holdings and Australian lead times.** Premium international brands entering the Australian market are not always holding local inventory. Lead times can vary significantly depending on origin, freight consolidation, and customs clearance. For a fit-out with a fixed opening date, that gap can be critical. Ask where stock is held, not where the supplier is based.

**Clarify delivery scope before you sign.** Drop-shipping a palletised order to a loading dock is not the same as on-site delivery with equipment positioned and ready for use. The distinction affects your opening timeline and your staff's workload. Ask whether installation is included, coordinated, or priced separately.

**Ask how co-branding is priced.** If bespoke sizing or branded plates are quoted as a customisation premium, that cost compounds across a multi-site rollout, so get the basis of the price in writing before you commit to a network spec.

**Read pricing transparency as a signal.** Suppliers who publish pricing openly are easier to budget around and tend to stand behind their specifications. A contact-form barrier often means the price shifts depending on how the conversation goes, which is a particular burden for independent operators comparing options without a procurement team.

For context on how supply chain complexity affects these questions, MasterKraft's guide to commercial gym fit-out in New Zealand illustrates how lead time and installation gaps compound when local support is thin.

## Franchise and Multi-Site Considerations That Get Overlooked

At network scale, every procurement decision compounds, and not every supplier is structured to handle that.

**Standardise the specification, not just the brand.** When every site in your network runs the same bumper plate, members moving between locations lift on identical equipment. Staff know what to inspect, what to order, and what to replace without referring upward. Maintenance becomes a system rather than a site-by-site judgement call.

**Structure procurement around site opening dates, not warehouse capacity.** A well-structured agreement with your supplier stages delivery to each site as it approaches opening, rather than releasing full stock on contract execution. This keeps capital working in your business rather than sitting in a warehouse. Confirm in writing that your supplier can hold allocated stock against a rollout schedule without requiring full prepayment on delivery.

**Negotiate co-branding into the network agreement rather than per order.** Franchise operators who treat branded equipment as a per-site customisation add-on pay an uplift each time, which erodes the benefit of network buying power. Settle the basis of that price once, at the volume tier. If you are working through the full capital picture, the guide on what it actually costs to open a gym in Australia covers where branded equipment sits in a realistic fit-out budget.

**Supplier track record at scale is an operational filter, not a marketing claim.** MasterKraft has fitted out 229 sites across 12 countries, covering equipment, flooring and storage, which is the kind of history that shows whether documentation, logistics coordination and post-installation support are built for network complexity.

**Write the specification into your franchise standard.** Define the minimum plate grade, construction spec, and approved supplier in your operations manual. This prevents future site operators from substituting cheaper alternatives that degrade the member experience and expose the network to liability.

## Transparent Pricing and What It Actually Signals About a Supplier

**Contact-form gatekeeping costs independent operators time they do not have.** When a gym owner budgeting a fit-out needs to compare plate specifications across three suppliers, a "request a quote" barrier on two of those sites adds days of lag to a decision that may already be under capital pressure. Transparent pricing on a product page removes that friction entirely.

Enterprise buyers can absorb this. An operations manager standardising equipment across 20 sites can schedule supplier calls and wait for formal quotes. An independent owner opening a single facility, often for the first time, cannot easily price a fit-out when much of the market keeps its numbers behind a form.

**Pricing transparency is also a proxy signal worth reading carefully.** A supplier confident in its product-to-price positioning tends to publish that positioning openly. A quote-only model is not automatically disqualifying, and there are legitimate reasons for it on large installed equipment, but operators should treat pricing visibility as one indicator of how a supplier positions itself and how quickly you can budget around it.

Aggressive promotional discounting is a separate signal. Deep sitewide sales on strength equipment are worth interrogating. Ask whether the discount reflects a clearance event, a change in stock, or simply how that supplier structures its list pricing.

**For budgeting purposes:** allow for a full standard weight range per platform, across the number of platforms your floor plan supports. Budget a contingency above per-plate cost to account for delivery, installation, and early replacement of the lightest plates, which manufacturers commonly warn should not be dropped on their own.

## Making the Right Call for Your Facility

Once you've worked through pricing, the final decision comes down to honest operational assessment.

**Specify for actual use, not aspirational programming.** A 24/7 facility running strength and functional training across six platforms at peak hours needs a different plate spec than a boutique studio with two platforms and a structured class timetable. Match your specification to real member volume and session intensity. Buying down to save capital and buying up to future-proof both carry risk; the right answer sits in an honest read of your current floor.

Evaluate suppliers on documented service commitment, a written SLA, confirmed local stock, and on-site delivery, not on promotional copy.

For franchise operators, plate specification set at the network level is a brand and logistics decision that compounds across every site.

MasterKraft publishes a 72-hour service SLA, in writing, covering response and resolution, and puts prices on its product pages rather than behind an enquiry form, with larger machines quoted on enquiry.

**Ready to move forward?** Review the MasterKraft bumper plate range online, or request a facility equipment quote for a new fit-out or network rollout.

## Conclusion

Getting specification and supplier selection right is an operational decision that determines how your floor performs over years of daily use. For franchise operators, the consequences of that decision compound across every site in the network.

Review the full range online today, or request a facility quote for your fit-out or network rollout. The right decision starts with the right conversation.

posts.title: The Commercial Gym Operator's Guide to Buying Kettlebells
posts.description: A practical buying guide for gym operators on commercial kettlebell selection, coating types, weight ranges, storage, and supplier evaluation.

heroImage.alt: The Commercial Gym Operator's Guide to Buying Kettlebells

posts.bodyMd:
Buying kettlebells for a commercial facility is nothing like buying them for personal use. Handle tolerances, coating durability, weight progression gaps, and total cost of ownership all carry consequences that compound over thousands of training sessions. A poor choice made at the purchase stage can mean damaged floors, inconsistent user experience, and premature equipment replacement.

The decisions that matter are made before the order goes in: grade, specification, weight range, storage, and what a supplier is willing to put in writing. Get them right and kettlebells become facility infrastructure rather than a recurring replacement line.

## Commercial Grade vs. Consumer Grade: Why the Difference Matters

![Commercial Grade vs. Consumer Grade: Why the Difference Matters](/blog-images/w8wtB5vIi6TdROHsCTZ76.webp "Commercial Grade vs. Consumer Grade: Why the Difference Matters")

Not all kettlebells are built for the same job. Consumer-grade bells are engineered for intermittent home use, typically one user, a few sessions per week, at modest rep volumes. Put that same equipment into a commercial facility where dozens of members cycle through every day and the engineering assumptions stop holding.

Commercial-grade kettlebells are manufactured to tighter dimensional tolerances: consistent handle diameter across the weight range, flat bases that sit stable under load, and predictable centre-of-gravity that allows coaches to build reliable progressions. These are not marketing distinctions; they are functional requirements for a multi-user environment where inconsistency creates injury risk and coaching friction.

Budget imports frequently clear initial inspection but degrade under commercial volume. Coating failures, handle roughness, and unfinished casting seams can surface well before the end of the expected service life, generating member complaints and coach workarounds that erode class experience well before the equipment fails completely. The lessons from long-term ROI analysis on commercial gym fit-outs apply directly here: under-specified equipment costs more over a facility lifecycle than the premium avoided at purchase.

Durability is not a capital cost in isolation. Equipment condition directly affects member retention, liability exposure, and facility reputation, making the grade of bell you buy a revenue decision as much as a procurement one.

## Handle Diameter, Finish, and Balance: The Specs That Actually Matter

Those dimensional tolerances translate directly into five specifications worth examining before you commit to a set.

**Handle diameter** is the starting point, and it is worth being precise about where a standard actually applies. Competition kettlebells are dimensionally standardised by the kettlebell sport governing bodies: the [IUKL specifies a 35mm handle](https://kettlebell.university/sport/rules/equipment/kb-dimensions/), the WKSF 34mm, the IKO 35mm plus or minus 1mm, and the GSU a 32mm to 35mm range. Those figures govern sanctioned competition equipment, not cast iron commercial bells, whose handle diameter commonly varies with bell weight. If you want one grip cue that works across your whole range, you need a matched set specified to a single handle diameter, and you need to ask for that figure rather than assume it.

**Handle finish** determines both grip feel and maintenance burden. Raw cast iron delivers a naturally textured surface that works well with chalk, but requires periodic oiling to prevent rust in humid environments. Powder coat is the more practical commercial choice, providing a cleanable, chip-resistant surface, provided application thickness is controlled. Overly thick powder coat rounds the handle profile and reduces grip security under load.

**Casting seams on the handle interior** are where budget bells fail first. A residual seam along the inner handle causes progressive callusing and skin tears during high-rep swings or cleans, generating member complaints that reflect on your sourcing decision rather than the equipment itself. Machine-finishing that removes seam material entirely is the baseline for commercial-grade acceptability.

**Centre-of-gravity consistency** across a matched set is non-negotiable for functional training studios. Coaches build progressions around predictable feel; variance between bells of the same nominal weight disrupts that precision.

**Window clearance**, the internal space between handle and bell body, determines whether a chalked or gloved hand and forearm pass through cleanly on a rack or a snatch. On cast iron ranges it varies between weight classes, so request the figure at the top of your intended range before ordering rather than after.

## Coating Options and Durability Under Daily Commercial Use

Coating choice is where commercial durability is won or lost.

**Powder coat** is the most practical finish for commercial facilities. It resists chipping under repeated drops, cleans readily with standard gym disinfectants, and is available in weight-specific colour systems that let members self-select the right bell without reading a number. That last point is more operationally significant than it sounds.

**Vinyl-coated bells** offer one genuine advantage: floor protection on drops. The trade-off is structural. Vinyl traps sweat and moisture at the seam between coating and cast iron, accelerating internal rust and causing delamination from the inside out. That is a durability trade made for the sake of the floor, so if drop protection is the problem you are solving, solve it in the flooring rather than the coating. Vinyl is a floor protection solution, not a durability solution.

**Raw cast iron** develops a patina that offers some protection over time and can stay serviceable for a long time with consistent care. The limitation is maintenance: periodic oiling is required, making raw iron poorly suited to high-humidity group fitness environments where consistent upkeep is unrealistic.

**Chrome-finished handles** carry aesthetic appeal but can lose surface consistency under repeated drops, making powder coat the more reliable default.

For facilities prioritising operational efficiency, colour-coded sets earn their place whatever the coating: they reduce class set-up time, minimise misracking, and produce a cleaner floor presentation. Competition bells are uniform in size and colour-coded by weight as standard, which is one reason coached studios often default to them. For a detailed look at how coating spec fits into broader equipment decisions, Commercial Gym Equipment Australia: How to Spec the Right Grade for Your Facility covers the full framework.

## Weight Range Recommendations by Facility Type

The following ranges reflect common commercial practice. Verify them against your own programming before committing.

Colour-coding tells your members which bell to grab; getting the weight range right tells you which bells to buy in the first place.

**Functional training studios and boutique group fitness facilities** should cover 8kg to 32kg, with the core working range between 12kg and 24kg for mixed-gender classes. That concentration is where your volume lands, so buying deeper in that window (multiples per weight) makes more sense than extending the range thinly.

**24/7 open-access gyms** need a broader spread, typically 4kg to 48kg. Without a coach cueing appropriate loading, members self-select across a wider range, and rehabilitation and general conditioning use cases pull the bottom of the range down to 4kg and 6kg more than a coached studio would.

**Corporate wellness facilities** skew lighter. A 4kg to 20kg set covers the majority of use cases, with priority on a visually clean, durable set that performs across a long lifecycle at lower daily volume.

**Multi-site franchise networks** should lock in a single weight range and bell specification across all locations. Consistent programming, no member confusion when visiting a different site, and straightforward reorder logistics all depend on it. This feeds directly into the real costs of opening and fitting out a gym in Australia that catch operators off-guard.

Regardless of facility type, buying complete matched sets from a single source protects dimensional consistency, ensures your storage rack fits correctly, and eliminates the handle variation that creates uneven coaching experiences. Browse MasterKraft's commercial mixed implements range to see full set options with transparent pricing.

## Storage, Racking, and Floor Space Planning for Kettlebell Zones

Once you've confirmed your weight range, storage planning determines whether that investment functions well on the floor or creates daily friction.

**Horizontal A-frame racks** are the most space-efficient format for commercial kettlebell storage. Bells sit in weight order at a visible angle, accessible without crouching, with a floor footprint significantly smaller than vertical or tiered shelf alternatives.

A set running 8kg to 48kg in 4kg increments is eleven bells, and it fits within a compact linear footprint, with exact dimensions varying by manufacturer specification. Confirm the rack's footprint and its bell capacity against your own set size rather than assuming the two match.

Zone positioning matters as much as the rack itself. Kettlebell areas should sit on rubber flooring rated for impact, with enough clear swing radius per user. Confirm the appropriate clearance with your fit-out partner or against the relevant safety guidance. For group class layouts, plan adequate spacing between stations for safe movement.

Rack and bell dimensions must match. Mismatched racking causes overhang, instability, and bells resting at angles that signal a poorly managed facility to new members. These are small details that shape first impressions at the point of joining.

MasterKraft's kettlebell storage solutions are specified alongside its bell range, so dimensional compatibility is built in rather than retrofitted. The result is a stable, visually coherent floor presentation without the guesswork of sourcing racking separately after the bells arrive.

## Total Cost of Ownership vs. Upfront Price

![Total Cost of Ownership vs. Upfront Price](/blog-images/JCINOZEEiOm7dyiRoxdUZ.webp "Total Cost of Ownership vs. Upfront Price")

Once your storage layout is sorted, the next question most operators ask is straightforward: can they save money by going cheaper on the bells themselves? Rarely, on an honest lifecycle view.

Budget-import kettlebells priced at a significant discount to commercial grade look compelling at the point of purchase. Under sustained commercial use, partial replacement can become necessary early enough to eliminate the original saving entirely and add a second freight and logistics cost on top. Model the replacement point against your own rep volume rather than against a generic lifecycle figure.

These quality failures generate member complaints and erode retention, costs that never appear on the original invoice.

**The variables to model when assessing total cost of ownership:**

- Replacement cycle length under your actual daily rep volume

- Freight cost for reorders, particularly for heavier weight sets

- Storage rack compatibility if replacement bells differ dimensionally from the originals

- Staff time spent fielding and managing member complaints about equipment condition

Commercial-grade bells backed by a documented service SLA and confirmed parts availability address the floor downtime risk directly. When a bell fails mid-programme cycle, a clear resolution timeline matters operationally.

MasterKraft's written 72-hour response and resolution SLA gives operators exactly that. Budget-import channels typically offer no equivalent support structure, leaving facility managers to absorb the problem internally with no defined path to resolution.

## Integrating Kettlebells Into a Complete Facility Design

Getting the right kettlebells onto your floor is one decision. Designing a zone where they actually perform is another.

Kettlebells function best as part of a cohesive training environment where flooring, storage, and functional rig placement are planned together rather than sourced in sequence and reconciled later. A dedicated kettlebell zone requires rubber flooring rated for impact absorption at a commercial-grade thickness. Check the rating against flooring specifications or with your fit-out partner. Anything below the appropriate rating risks damage to the subfloor structure and to the bells themselves from routine drops during swings, cleans and snatches.

The ongoing growth of boutique studios and hybrid fitness models is reinforcing exactly this kind of integrated thinking. Operators in constrained footprints need implements that serve multiple programming needs without consuming disproportionate floor space, and kettlebells are one of the few categories that deliver that. The demand is real, and so is the planning complexity that comes with it.

Where operators lose time and money is in managing multiple vendor timelines: one supplier for bells, another for flooring, a third for storage racking, a fourth for the rig. Each introduces a separate lead time, a separate installation sequence, and a separate accountability gap when something does not fit.

A single supplier capable of specifying all of those elements under one project scope eliminates that overhead. MasterKraft's fit-out service covers equipment, storage, flooring, and installation as a single scope, whether you are a franchise network standardising a new site or an independent operator refurbishing an existing one. Browse the current product range and available stock to see what is available for immediate specification.

## What to Ask a Kettlebell Supplier Before You Order

Once your fit-out design is locked, the next risk sits with your supplier. These five questions separate credible commercial suppliers from catalogue vendors.

1. **Request full dimensional specification sheets** covering handle diameter, window clearance, base diameter, and overall height across the entire weight range. Marketing images typically feature mid-range bells. The 8kg and 48kg ends of the set are where dimensional shortcuts show up.

2. **Confirm the casting method and seam-finishing process.** Machine-finished handles with minimal residual casting seam are a meaningful quality marker. Ask any supplier to confirm their finishing process in writing.

3. **Check whether pricing is published or quote-only.** Transparent pricing removes a friction point from your budget approval process. MasterKraft lists prices on its kettlebell product pages, including set and rack packages; larger machines elsewhere in the catalogue are quoted on enquiry.

4. **Ask about lead times for full sets, delivery, installation support, and warranty claims.** Specifically, ask what happens if a bell arrives damaged or fails within the warranty period. A documented SLA is the answer you need. Verbal reassurance is not.

5. **Confirm commercial fit-out experience at volume.** Request references from multi-site operators or franchise networks. Volume supply experience indicates supply chain reliability and consistent specification across large orders. For context on why this matters across the full procurement process, the four-phase gym fit-out framework covering scope, spec, supply and support is worth reviewing before finalising any supplier decision.

## Conclusion: Making the Right Call on Kettlebells for Your Facility

Once you have asked the right questions and received satisfactory answers, the procurement decision becomes straightforward.

One principle carries the whole decision: **commercial-grade specification, matched sets and a supplier with a documented service SLA are what make the numbers work over the life of the equipment, not the lowest purchase price.** The upfront saving evaporates at the first replacement cycle, and it takes costs with it that never appeared on the original invoice.

Treat kettlebell procurement as facility infrastructure, not consumables. Require dimensional specs and SLA documentation before committing, the same way you would for flooring or rig anchoring.

MasterKraft's kettlebell product pages carry prices, including set and rack packages, so comparisons and budget approvals do not have to wait on a contact form. For operators planning a broader refurbishment, the fit-out consultation pathway covers equipment, storage, flooring, and installation under a single project scope.

MasterKraft supplies single independent studios and national franchise rollouts on the same specification terms. Ask for the dimensional sheets and the SLA in writing, and compare them against whatever else you are considering.

posts.title: How the Australian Gym Equipment Market Really Works
posts.description: Understand Australia's 3-tier gym equipment market, why independents get trapped, and what commercial-grade mid-market supply actually looks like.

heroImage.alt: How the Australian Gym Equipment Market Really Works

posts.bodyMd:
Most gym operators approach equipment procurement the wrong way. They search for a product, compare a few prices, and assume the market works like any other retail category. It does not, and that misunderstanding costs Australian gym businesses time, money, and operational reliability every year.

The Australian commercial gym equipment sector is more fragmented than most operators realise. The choices available to you are not equal, and neither are the risks attached to each one. What looks like a straightforward purchasing decision is actually a strategic one, shaped by supplier tiers, service gaps, and a structural false choice that traps independent operators.

![Why "Gym Equipment" Is the Wrong Starting Question](/blog-images/RVAbtNNqO2u8tC5bx_z8G.webp "Why Gym Equipment Is the Wrong Starting Question")

## Why "Gym Equipment" Is the Wrong Starting Question

Most operators begin their gym equipment search the same way: opening multiple supplier websites and comparing product catalogues. It feels like the logical starting point. It is not. The procurement decision is largely made before a single item is quoted, and it is made at the supplier level, not the product level.

The questions that actually determine facility ROI have nothing to do with frame dimensions or weight stack increments. They are: what happens when something fails, who installs the equipment and is accountable for the outcome, how long does delivery realistically take, and can you get a price without submitting a contact form and waiting for a discovery call? These are supplier operating model questions, and most operators never ask them until something goes wrong.

The structure of the Australian market compounds this problem. Suppliers range from global manufacturers to single-showroom retailers to refurbished-stock dealers, and their catalogue language is largely interchangeable. Navigating that purely on equipment specifications produces decisions that look sound on paper and underperform on the floor.

The fragmentation matters because it obscures structural differences between suppliers that are far more consequential than any product specification. A supplier's installation capability, written service commitments, and pricing accessibility tell you more about how a facility will operate in year two than any spec sheet reviewed in year zero.

Reframing the search around supplier capability, service commitments, and total cost of ownership does not mean ignoring product quality. It means applying the correct filter first, so that product evaluation happens within a shortlist of suppliers who can actually support a commercial facility rather than across every catalogue in the market.

## How the Australian Market Breaks Into Three Tiers

Once you accept that supplier selection precedes product selection, the next question is structural: which kind of supplier are you actually dealing with?

The Australian commercial gym equipment market divides into three tiers, and each has a distinct logic that determines pricing, service model, and suitability for different facility types.

### Tier 1: Enterprise-Grade Premium

Suppliers at this level, Life Fitness being the most prominent example, carry decades of operational history. Life Fitness was founded in 1977 and states that it operates in over 120 countries. Their engineering reflects the full breadth of that client base: hospital rehabilitation facilities, hotel fitness centres, and corporate wellness programmes sit alongside performance gyms in their design brief. The result is equipment built to institutional procurement standards, with pricing and support structures calibrated accordingly. For a 200-member independent gym, that institutional overhead is largely wasted capital.

### Tier 2: Mass-Market Retail

Dynamo Fitness lists 14 stores across five states. Verve Fitness states over 16,000 commercial fitouts completed and over 3,000 verified customer reviews. Both compete on catalogue breadth, physical presence, and volume. Those are genuine assets, but neither catalogue breadth nor review volume tells you what happens when a machine fails, so ask each supplier directly for a written response and resolution commitment. Specialist manufacturers such as AlphaFit and Vulcan Fitness also sell into this space.

### Tier 3: Budget and Refurbished

Operators like Grays Fitness specialise in used and refurbished commercial fitness equipment, serving facilities with constrained budgets or temporary setups. The constraint is remaining service life. Refurbished stock has already spent part of its working life elsewhere, and a high-utilisation facility cycling members through equipment daily will consume the rest of it faster than a low-traffic site will. Establish the age, service history and warranty position of every unit before procurement, not after. The real costs of opening a gym in Australia rarely account for accelerated replacement cycles from underspecified equipment.

### Geography and the Fragmentation Opportunity

Across all three tiers, fragmentation remains high, which creates a real advantage for suppliers with national delivery and professional installation capability rather than showroom-dependent models. For operators outside major metro areas, the question of who physically installs the equipment is not academic. A review of completed gym fitouts across Australia illustrates what that national delivery and installation footprint looks like in practice.

The first filter any operator should apply is simple: identify which tier a supplier actually occupies, not which tier their marketing implies. The language used to describe product quality, value, and service varies far less between tiers than the actual delivery models do.

## The False Choice Trapping Independent Operators

Knowing which tier a supplier occupies is the first filter. The harder problem is what happens once an independent operator or challenger franchise actually tries to buy.

The market structure creates a binary that looks like a choice but functions like a trap. Tier 1 engineering is built for institutional procurement: hospital rehabilitation facilities, hotel chains, and enterprise health clubs with capital budgets, procurement teams, and utilisation profiles that justify the price point. A 200-member independent gym in regional Queensland does not have those margins, and locking budget into that tier leaves less capital for flooring, lighting, functional zones, and the fit-out elements that actually move the needle on member acquisition. The cost of over-engineering is not abstract; it is the rig you could not afford, the lighting that stayed basic, the functional training zone that never got built.

The cost of going the other direction is equally concrete, just distributed differently across time. Flat-pack Tier 3 imports carry their real price in failure rates, not in the purchase invoice. A cable machine that fails under real member loads during a Monday evening peak is not a maintenance line item. It is a membership complaint logged that night, a class cancellation the following morning, and a facility reputation event that circulates on local social media before the repair quote arrives. Neither the safety exposure nor the damage to member trust appears in the original purchase comparison.

What makes this trap effective is that it is invisible at the point of purchase. Suppliers present these tiers as "quality" versus "value," which sounds like a reasonable spectrum. It obscures the structural reality: both ends of that spectrum carry costs for operators sitting outside the institutional procurement bracket.

This is the operating reality MasterKraft is built around. The catalogue sits at commercial-grade durability because the engineering is sized for real member utilisation, not institutional over-specification. The pricing is set for operators making capital decisions without procurement teams behind them.

The false choice dissolves when the third option is actually built, rather than just described.

![What a Commercial-Grade Middle Market Actually Looks Like](/blog-images/8re08RAWuQW8OnAcsMBSI.webp "What a Commercial-Grade Middle Market Actually Looks Like")

## What a Commercial-Grade Middle Market Actually Looks Like

So what does the middle actually deliver, in concrete terms?

**Commercial-grade in this context means equipment engineered for real utilisation loads**, daily multi-user volume, chalk, sweat, dropped weights, peak-hour throughput, without the institutional over-engineering sized for hospital rehabilitation facilities or hotel chains. ISO 20957 is the relevant reference point: it classifies stationary training equipment by intended use, with class S covering professional and commercial application and class H covering home use. It sets no frame steel gauge, so treat a quoted gauge as a marketing number rather than a standards claim, and ask instead which ISO 20957 class the equipment is built and certified to.

### TCO Is the Only Honest Metric

Purchase price is a poor unit of comparison when the real cost plays out over 36 months on the gym floor. A cable machine purchased at a lower price point that requires significant repair or replacement under commercial loads carries a higher total cost of ownership than one purchased at a higher initial price with a documented service commitment behind it. That replacement cycle is invisible in a purchase order and very visible on a P&L.

If you want to spec equipment to your actual usage load rather than to a price point, TCO is the framework that makes the comparison honest.

### Bespoke and Transparent as Standard

Bespoke sizing and co-branding should be included in the base offering, not quoted as customisation premiums. Franchise operators and independents building a brand identity are not asking for something exceptional; they are asking for equipment that represents their facility correctly. Charging extra for that is a supplier model designed around large procurement teams who absorb negotiation friction, not around operators making direct capital decisions.

Prices published on product pages, with larger machines quoted on enquiry, remove most of the discovery overhead that weighs heaviest on solo operators.

That is not a feature list. It is a supplier model built around how independent operators actually make decisions with real capital on the line.

## The Service Gap Nobody Is Talking About

Transparent pricing removes one procurement barrier. It does not remove the one that hits hardest after the purchase order is signed.

Post-sale support is often described only as a contact page or a phone number, with no stated response time attached. Whether a given supplier publishes a written service SLA is something to check directly on your own shortlist, because it is not something you can infer from the size of the catalogue or the review count.

The practical consequence matters more than the observation. "Contact us for support" is not a service commitment. It is a risk transfer. The supplier retains discretion over response speed, resolution scope, and escalation priority. The operator absorbs the operational exposure of that discretion during every hour a piece of revenue-critical equipment is out of service.

### Why Post-Sale Service Determines Facility ROI

A facility that loses a cable stack or a row of treadmills for two weeks during a drawn-out resolution process does not recover that period cleanly. Members notice. Classes get cancelled or restructured. Complaints accumulate. Some members do not renew. None of that appears on a product specification sheet, but all of it is a direct consequence of the service model sitting behind the product. Pre-sale specifications describe equipment performance under normal conditions. Post-sale service determines facility performance under the conditions that actually stress the operator relationship.

MasterKraft publishes a 72-hour service SLA, in writing, covering response and resolution. A cable stack failing at 6pm on a Tuesday is not a scheduled maintenance event with a flexible timeline. It is a facility problem with member-facing consequences that begin accumulating immediately, and a stated 72-hour window tells an operator what to expect. Operators fitting out facilities across the Tasman face a sharper version of the same question, because supply chains are longer and local support is thinner.

Before signing any purchase order with an Australian gym equipment supplier, ask one question: what is your written service response and resolution commitment? The answer, or the absence of one, tells you more about how that supplier will behave when something goes wrong than any catalogue, review count, or founding year narrative they lead with.

## Franchise Networks vs. Independent Operators: Same Standards, Different Scale

The service gap matters most when equipment is already down. But the preceding question, for any operator evaluating a supplier, is whether that supplier is structured to serve them at all, or whether their order size quietly determines the quality of process they receive.

### What Franchise Networks Actually Require

[Large franchise networks](https://getbizzie.com.au/blog/best-franchise-to-buy-in-australia) and multi-site operators, spanning 24/7 gym formats, boutique studios, health clubs, and pilates and functional training brands, face a supply problem that is fundamentally about replication. A fitout delivered to Site 1 must be reproducible at Site 14 without degradation in quality, timeline, or installation standard. That demands documented delivery and installation processes, not good intentions. Suppliers without that process infrastructure fail franchise networks not on product quality but on consistency, and inconsistency in a franchise model is a brand and compliance liability.

### What the Market Actually Delivers to Independents

Independent operators opening or refurbishing a single facility need exactly the same things: commercial-grade equipment, professional installation with accountable people on site, and a service commitment that holds when something goes wrong. What the market typically delivers instead is proportionate attention. Lower order volume means slower response, less rigorous installation support, and in many cases higher effective pricing because independents cannot negotiate volume terms. The result is that the operator who most needs a reliable supplier is the one most likely to receive a pallet at the kerb and a phone number.

### One Operating Model for Both

MasterKraft's deployment across 229 sites in 12 countries provides the documented scale evidence that franchise networks require before committing a supplier to a rollout programme. The operating model, however, is not tiered by order size. A single independent order runs through the same delivery, installation, and commissioning process as a national rollout. An independent gym owner in regional New South Wales receives professional on-site installation, not a flat-pack delivery. That is the standard franchise networks have always demanded; it is the standard independents rarely receive from the broader market.

### Complete Scope, Not Equipment Only

Fitout scope matters here because partial suppliers create coordination risk. MasterKraft's fitout scope covers equipment, flooring and storage, across a catalogue organised into 12 categories. Both franchise networks and independent operators need a complete facility, not a catalogue selection dropped into a space someone else has to finish. Single-supplier scope closes the accountability gap that partial fitouts create.

## Why the Operator Background of Your Supplier Matters

A supplier's catalogue tells you what they sell. Their operational background tells you whether they understand what you're buying it for, and that distinction matters far more than most operators realise until something goes wrong.

Across the Australian commercial gym equipment market, the dominant credibility signals are heritage metrics. Founding year, countries served, review volume. These are verifiable numbers, but they answer a different question than the one a facility operator is actually asking. Knowing that a brand has decades of history or has supplied facilities across multiple continents does not tell you what happens at 6pm on a Tuesday when a cable stack goes down during peak hour and you have members waiting.

The gap between those two questions is where operational experience becomes the actual differentiator.

A supplier who has managed a gym has stood in front of that problem. They have made the call about whether to pull the equipment from the floor, improvise a workaround, or absorb the member complaints while waiting on a resolution. They have also made the capital allocation decisions that their customers are currently facing: which zones to prioritise, how to sequence a fitout so the facility generates revenue before every piece of equipment arrives, why co-branding matters to a franchise operator building site consistency across a network. That accumulated knowledge changes the quality of advice at every point in the procurement process, in ways that a product specification sheet cannot reflect.

**MasterKraft positions itself explicitly on this background**, describing its team as real operators, people who have actually run training floors, and pointing to its written service commitment as the consequence of that.

The practical test is whether a supplier will put a number on it. MasterKraft publishes a 72-hour service SLA, in writing, covering response and resolution. A supplier who cannot state a response and resolution window at all is leaving the timing to its own discretion and the consequences to yours.

## What to Demand From Any Australian Gym Equipment Supplier

Knowing what separates a capable supplier from a costly one matters more at the shortlist stage than after you have signed a purchase order. These six questions cut through catalogue marketing and surface how a supplier actually operates.

**Can you get a price without submitting a contact form?** Friction at the pricing stage signals friction at every stage that follows. Ask before you shortlist.

**Is there a written service SLA, and is it published?** Ask for the written response and resolution timeline. The presence or absence of a published SLA tells you more than any catalogue does.

**Is installation performed by people on site?** Kerb delivery shifts accountability entirely to you: fitout timelines slip, commissioning problems go unresolved, and insurance liability for incorrect installation sits with the operator. Professional installation means people on site who own the outcome, not a driver who hands over a pallet.

**Are bespoke sizing and co-branding included or quoted separately?** Franchise operators and independents building a brand identity should not carry a customisation premium for equipment that correctly represents their facility. Ask the question before you receive a quote, because the answer changes the real cost of the order.

**Does the supplier cover the complete facility?** Flooring, storage, functional zones, cardio, and strength from a single supplier eliminates the coordination gaps and accountability disputes that arise when multiple contractors share a fitout. If your supplier covers equipment but stops at the loading dock, you are managing the integration risk yourself.

**What is the actual deployment record?** A product catalogue labelled "commercial" is not a track record. Ask how many completed facilities the supplier can reference, across what formats (boutique studios, 24/7 gyms, franchise networks, health clubs), and at what geographic scale. Two hundred and twenty-nine sites across 12 countries represents a documented evidence base. A catalogue with a commercial label does not.

These are not aspirational standards. They are the minimum an operator should expect before committing capital to a supplier relationship, and they are questions the market currently leaves largely unanswered.

## Choosing a Gym Equipment Supplier With Confidence

Three criteria cut through the noise most reliably: transparent pricing, a written service SLA, and complete fitout capability. If a supplier cannot show you a price without a discovery call, cannot document their response and resolution commitment, and cannot cover the full facility scope, they are transferring risk onto you at every one of those gaps.

MasterKraft is built for the middle of this market. Prices sit on product pages rather than behind a form, with larger machines quoted on enquiry. The 72-hour service SLA is published in writing and covers response and resolution. Fitout scope covers equipment, flooring and storage. Bespoke sizing and co-branding are included as standard, not priced as extras.

Whether you are a national franchise or an independent owner, MasterKraft applies the same delivery, installation, and commissioning process, the same standard the 229-site deployment history was built on.

Browse the MasterKraft catalogue, organised into 12 categories with prices on the product pages and larger machines quoted on enquiry, explore the fitout planning resources to scope your facility properly, and reach out when you are ready to move. The process is the same for every operator.

## Conclusion

The Australian gym equipment market rewards operators who ask the right questions before signing anything. Understand the three tiers before you compare prices. Reject the false choice between consumer-grade affordability and enterprise-scale minimums. Demand written service commitments, not verbal reassurances. And choose a supplier whose operational background matches the environment your equipment will actually face.

The difference between a facility that retains members and one that quietly loses them often comes down to a single procurement decision made under time pressure.

posts.title: Commercial Dumbbells: A Gym Owner's Buying Guide
posts.description: Commercial dumbbells guide for gym owners: choose rubber hex, urethane, or adjustable options. Learn what separates quality from cheap imports.

heroImage.alt: Training with a dumbbell in a MasterKraft-equipped studio, dumbbell rack and kettlebells behind

posts.bodyMd:
Choosing the right dumbbells for a commercial gym is one of the most consequential purchasing decisions you will make. Get it right and you have equipment that withstands years of heavy daily use, keeps members satisfied, and protects your investment. Get it wrong and you are replacing warped handles, cracked coatings, and stripped knurling within 18 months.

Members who train regularly know what good equipment feels like, and substandard dumbbells will not go unnoticed.

Commercial dumbbell procurement comes down to four decisions: the coating and construction specified, the weight range committed to, the storage planned alongside it, and the supplier accountability secured before signing.

## Rubber Hex Dumbbells

Rubber hex dumbbells are one of the most widely used dumbbell types across Australian commercial gyms, and for good reason. They sit at the intersection of durability, cost-efficiency, and floor safety, making them the practical default for most facility types.

The hexagonal head design does specific work. It prevents dumbbells from rolling away after a set, reduces floor and rack damage on impact, and absorbs repeated drops better than chrome or cast iron alternatives. In a high-volume free weight zone, that geometry matters operationally.

**Where quality diverges is in the rubber itself.** Vulcanised rubber coating varies significantly between commercial-grade units and cheap imports. The most common failure points in budget product lines are surface cracking, delamination where the rubber separates from the head, and persistent off-gassing odour in enclosed spaces. These are not cosmetic issues; delaminating heads create a member safety concern and an early replacement cost that erodes any unit price saving.

Commercial-grade rubber hex dumbbells are best suited to functional training areas, free weight zones, and any facility where dumbbells cycle through multiple users daily. A 24/7 gym with 300-plus members will stress-test a dumbbell set far harder than a boutique studio, and the coating specification needs to reflect that.

Most commercial sets are configured from 2.5kg or 5kg up to 50kg, in 2.5kg or 5kg increments. Strength-focused facilities often extend the range beyond 50kg. MasterKraft's commercial gym equipment products include rubber hex options specified for exactly this kind of high-rotation environment.

## Urethane Dumbbells

Where rubber hex prioritises durability and value, urethane steps up for facilities where presentation is as important as performance.

Urethane is a harder, more abrasion-resistant compound than rubber. Under the daily cycle of drops, rack contact, and cleaning that commercial dumbbells endure, that hardness translates directly to surface longevity. Urethane maintains its colour and finish far longer than rubber when exposed to UV light and commercial-grade disinfectants, which degrade rubber coatings faster than urethane. For a facility wiping down equipment multiple times daily, that resistance is not cosmetic; it is structural.

The upfront cost is higher than rubber hex. The trade-off to weigh is that higher purchase price against how often the coating will need replacing in your specific environment, and each replacement cycle carries operational disruption as well as capital cost.

The smooth, consistent surface of urethane opens another commercial advantage: co-branding. Laser engraving and custom colour matching are both achievable on urethane with reliable results. Rubber does not hold engraving cleanly or accept colour consistently, making it a poor substrate for branded equipment. For franchise networks or boutique operators building a coherent facility identity, this matters across every site.

Urethane is the specified choice for boutique studios, health clubs, Pilates facilities, and functional training brands where member experience and room aesthetic are core parts of the offer. MasterKraft lists polyurethane dumbbells with prices on the product page.

## Chrome and Cast Iron Dumbbells

Where urethane suits premium presentation and longevity, chrome and cast iron occupy a more specific niche: lighter-weight ranges where aesthetics and compact storage matter more than drop-resistance.

Chrome dumbbells remain a traditional fixture in health clubs and rehabilitation spaces. Their slim profile fits neatly into tight free weight areas, and the clean aesthetic complements a studio environment in a way rubber hex cannot match. They work particularly well as a lighter-weight complement to a primary rubber hex set, covering the 2.5kg to 20kg range where members rarely drop from height.

Cast iron holds up adequately at lower weights, but at heavier weights the increased head size makes cast iron awkward to handle and harder on commercial flooring.

**The critical environmental limitation is humidity.** Chrome plating chips and rusts under sustained moisture exposure, making these dumbbells unsuitable for outdoor areas, covered courts, or facilities with poor ventilation. If your facility has any of these conditions, chrome should not be your primary dumbbell specification.

**When evaluating chrome suppliers, inspect two things first:** chrome plating thickness and knurling depth. Thin plating wears through within months of commercial use; shallow knurling reduces grip security and signals a budget manufacturing specification across the entire unit. A supplier who cannot provide coating specifications on request is not meeting commercial-grade procurement standards.

## Adjustable and Selectorised Dumbbells

Where chrome and cast iron suit fixed lighter-weight applications, adjustable dumbbells solve a different problem entirely: floor space.

A single adjustable unit can replace a substantial portion of a fixed-weight set, making the format practical for personal training zones, PT studios, or any facility where a full dumbbell rack is not viable. The trade-off is mechanical complexity, and that trade-off matters considerably in a commercial context.

**Selectorised designs** (pin-select or dial mechanisms) are meaningfully faster to adjust than plate-loaded alternatives, which makes them better suited to semi-commercial environments where multiple users cycle through the same equipment. For a PT bay where two or three clients train sequentially, selectorised units are a reasonable specification.

The durability risk is the mechanism itself. On lower-grade products, the adjustment assembly wears out under daily multi-user cycling long before the weight plates show any degradation. This is not a recoverable failure; a broken selector renders the unit unusable rather than just cosmetically worn.

**Adjustable dumbbells are not a viable sole dumbbell solution for a high-volume 24/7 facility.** They work well as a space-efficient supplement alongside a fixed rubber hex or urethane range, which handles the main floor volume.

One further consideration for commercial operators: much of the marketing for adjustable dumbbells is written for home users, where a single unit replacing a whole rack is the entire value proposition. Before over-indexing on this format, evaluate your actual member usage. A flat bench paired with a compact fixed-weight range will serve most commercial PT zones more reliably than adjustable units alone.

## Fixed Weight Sets vs. Modular Ranges

Where adjustable formats fall short on volume, fixed weight sets pick up the load.

A **fixed set spanning 5kg to 50kg in 2.5kg or 5kg increments**, paired with a matched rack, is the standard commercial specification for good reason: it is straightforward to manage, easy to replace individual pairs, and delivers a consistent member experience from day one.

For independents opening a first site with capital constraints, a **modular approach** is a practical alternative. Start with a core weight band, say 5kg to 30kg, and expand incrementally as membership grows. It avoids the upfront cost of a complete set while keeping the facility functional.

One critical caution: an incomplete range is an easily avoidable source of member complaints. A strength-focused gym that stops at 30kg, or has 10kg gaps between heavier pairs, signals under-investment and frustrates experienced members. Plan your ceiling weight before you open, even if you phase the purchase.

**Storage rack selection must be specified alongside the dumbbell range, not after the fact.** Tree racks, three-tier horizontal racks, and saddle-style racks suit different floor layouts and member flow patterns. Retrofitting the wrong rack wastes space and creates congestion. Browse equipment storage options early in the planning process.

Finally, if you are phasing a modular rollout, confirm that future weight additions from the same supplier will match the **head diameter and handle length** of your existing set. Mixing suppliers mid-range creates inconsistent rack fit and an unprofessional aesthetic that is difficult to reverse.

## What Separates Commercial-Grade Dumbbells from Cheap Imports

Choosing the right set is only half the equation. How that set is built determines whether it survives commercial use.

**Common failure modes on cheap import dumbbells** follow a consistent pattern: rubber delamination, handles loosening under repeated loading, inaccurate weight labelling, and coating off-gassing in poorly ventilated spaces. Each follows predictably from budget manufacturing specifications.

**Commercial-grade construction** addresses each at the source. Look for solid steel handle cores, which resist flex under load. Weight tolerance held close to stated weight keeps progressive overload programmes accurate. Vulcanised or urethane coatings bonded directly to the head, rather than overmoulded, maintain adhesion under the thermal cycling and cleaning chemical exposure that commercial environments produce daily.

The hidden cost of flat-pack imports is not the unit price; it is the replacement cycle. When a batch fails, there is no installation support, no service SLA, and no supplier accountability. That price saving disappears quickly.

For commercial operators, a published response and resolution commitment is a meaningful operational safeguard. Downtime in a free weight zone drives member complaints, and in a 24/7 facility there is no staffed window to manage them.

When evaluating any supplier, request load testing documentation, coating specifications, handle torque ratings, and references from comparable commercial installations. A credible supplier provides all of these without hesitation.

## How to Spec Dumbbells for Your Facility

Identifying commercial-grade product is only part of the task; speccing the right product for your facility before you order is equally important.

**Start with your member profile.** A 24/7 strength gym typically warrants a heavier upper range than a Pilates or barre studio, where lighter weights predominate. Getting this wrong means over-spending on spec you do not need, or under-building and replacing product ahead of schedule.

**Estimate usage volume per pair.** A high-volume facility will cycle each dumbbell pair through far more drop, rack, and clean events weekly than a smaller boutique. Higher cycle volume demands heavier coating bonds and solid-core handles. Build this into your material selection, not as an afterthought.

**Plan storage before you finalise the dumbbell type.** A vertical tree rack requires clear aisle depth and managed traffic flow that a three-tier horizontal rack does not. Locking in your floor plan first prevents costly rework. For a broader look at matching equipment spec to your actual usage load, the facility spec guide covers this in detail.

**Budget for the full set from day one.** Partial sets create member friction immediately and force a second procurement event when capital is typically tighter than at opening.

**For franchise and multi-site operators**, custom-engraved or colour-matched dumbbells are achievable at commercial order volumes and lock in brand consistency across every site.

## MasterKraft's Dumbbell Range

Once you have your specification mapped, the next step is sourcing from a supplier built for commercial reality rather than retail convenience.

MasterKraft supplies rubber hex, polyurethane, and chrome dumbbell ranges specified for commercial use. Prices sit on product pages rather than behind a form, with larger machines quoted on enquiry, so operators can evaluate fit against budget before a conversation starts. ## Choosing the Right Dumbbells for Your Gym

Getting the specification right before you purchase prevents most of the costly errors gym owners make on free weights.

1. **Match type to facility first.** Rubber hex suits high-volume, multi-user environments; urethane suits boutique and studio settings where finish longevity and aesthetics matter; chrome works for lighter-weight health club and rehab applications; adjustable formats suit PT zones, not primary free weight floors. Unit price is not a criterion until type is confirmed.
2. **Specify weight range and storage together.** Rack selection, floor clearance, and traffic flow are all determined by the weight range you commit to, and retrofitting costs more than planning correctly from the outset.
3. **Evaluate suppliers on documentation, installation, and SLA.** A credible supplier produces load testing results, coating specifications, and handle torque ratings without hesitation, and a written response and resolution commitment is a meaningful commercial benchmark.

heroImage.alt: A garage home gym with bench, bike, rower and wall storage

posts.bodyMd:
Most home gyms fail quietly. Nobody gets hurt and nothing breaks. The room just stops getting used, because the bench lives in front of the car, the dumbbells live on the floor, and setting up for a session takes longer than the session.

The fix is rarely more equipment. It is planning the room before buying anything for it. This guide works through that in the order that matters: space, floor, core kit, storage, then the extras.

## Start with the room, not the catalogue

Measure the space you actually have, then subtract what the room still has to do. A garage that still needs to fit a car is a very different brief from a spare room that can be given over completely.

Three measurements decide most of what follows:

- **Clear floor area.** The rectangle you can train in without moving anything. A bench and a set of dumbbells need far less than a rack and barbell, which need space for the bar to pass through on both sides.
- **Ceiling height.** Overhead pressing and pull-ups need clearance above your reach, not just above your head. Low garage ceilings and roller-door tracks catch a lot of people out.
- **Wall space.** Walls are where a small gym finds its room. Plates, bands, bars and accessories that hang up are floor space you get back.

If you are not sure what fits, mark the footprint of each piece on the floor with tape before you buy. It costs nothing and it settles most arguments.

## Protect the floor first

Concrete garage floors are hard on dropped weights, and dropped weights are hard on concrete. Timber and tiled floors in a spare room are less forgiving still.

Rubber gym flooring under the training area does three jobs at once. It protects the slab or the floorboards. It protects the equipment, because a dumbbell landing on rubber takes far less punishment than one landing on concrete. And it gives you stable footing, which matters more than people expect once the weights get heavier.

You do not need to cover the whole room. Cover the zones where weights get set down or dropped: around the dumbbell rack, under the bench and anywhere you lift from the floor.

## The core kit: what to buy first

A home gym that gets used is usually built around a short list, bought well:

1. **A set of dumbbells you will not outgrow quickly.** Dumbbells cover pressing, rowing, squatting, hinging and carrying, so they do more work per square metre than anything else you can buy. Start with the weights you use most, and plan for the heavier pairs you will want later. Our [guide to fixed and adjustable dumbbells](/blog/fixed-vs-adjustable-dumbbells-home-gym) covers which type suits which room.
2. **An adjustable bench.** A good adjustable bench turns a dumbbell set into a full program: flat, incline and seated work from one footprint. Look for a published load rating and real seat adjustment. MasterKraft's adjustable utility weight bench is rated to 400kg, with four backrest positions (flat, 30, 45 and 65 degrees) and three seat positions.
3. **Somewhere to put it all.** Covered next, because it is where most home gyms go wrong.

After that, add to the room based on how you train. A rack and barbell suit people chasing heavy strength work. Kettlebells, a rower or a bike suit people training for conditioning. Buy the second wave once the first is earning its place.

## Storage is what makes the room usable

Equipment on the floor turns a gym into a storeroom. The single biggest difference between a home gym that gets used and one that does not is whether everything has a place to go.

- **Dumbbell racks** keep the weights off the floor and in order. A vertical rack stores pairs in a small footprint, which suits tight rooms. A horizontal two-tier rack holds a longer run of pairs at an easy height to grab and return.
- **Wall storage** handles plates, bars, bands and accessories. In a garage, a wall rail or plate holders can free up more floor than any other change you make.
- **Modular storage racks** suit mixed kit, such as kettlebells and dumbbells, or medicine balls, on one frame.

Buy storage at the same time as the equipment, and size it for the set you plan to own, not just the set you are buying today. A rack that is full on day one needs a second rack the first time you add a pair.

## Buy once, buy commercial grade where it counts

Home equipment does not take the punishment a commercial floor does, but it does have to last. And the cheapest kit is often the kit you end up replacing.

Spend where failure is expensive or unsafe: anything you lie under, sit on or load heavily, such as the bench, rack and bars. Spend where the coating takes the wear, such as dumbbells and plates. Save on accessories that are easy to replace.

MasterKraft builds commercial-grade equipment that is also sold for home gyms: the same benches, dumbbells and storage that go into the studios we fit out, scaled to the room you have.

## Get the room planned before you buy

If you would rather have the layout worked out for you, our [home gym fit-out service](/fitout/home-gym-fitout) starts with your space and your training, then recommends the kit and the storage to fit both.

And if you want it in before the end of the year, last orders close **Saturday 31 October**. Prices are on the product pages, so you can plan the room tonight.

posts.title: How to Choose a Commercial Gym Fit-Out Partner on the Gold Coast
posts.description: Cut through the noise of Gold Coast gym fit-out suppliers. A practical guide for operators on the 5 criteria that actually matter before you sign anything.
